name: Buffy Wicks
title: California State Assemblymember, Chair of the Assembly Appropriations Committee
district: California State Assembly District 14 (East Bay: Oakland, Berkeley, Richmond, El Cerrito, San Pablo, Piedmont; represented as District 15 from 2018 to 2022 before redistricting)
years_of_service: December 3, 2018 to present (District 15, 2018 to 2022; District 14, 2022 to present). Her current term ends December 7, 2026. She advanced from the June 2, 2026 top-two primary (81.3% of the vote) and is on the November 3, 2026 general-election ballot against Green Party candidate Mark Rendon for a fifth term.
background: Wicks earned a B.A. in political science and government from the University of Washington in 1999. Her career before the Assembly included founding the political consultancy Rise Strategies, LLC; serving as California campaign director of Common Sense Kids Action; serving as executive director of Priorities USA Action; and serving as deputy director of the White House Office of Public Engagement under President Barack Obama, a role her official biography describes as six years working for the Obama administration. She was also a fellow with the Institute of Politics and Public Service at Georgetown University. (Sources: Ballotpedia, Buffy Wicks; official Assembly biography, wicks.asmdc.org/biography.)

Wicks was first elected in 2018 to the open Assembly District 15 seat in a crowded 12-candidate Democratic field, winning the June 5, 2018 primary with 31.4% and then defeating fellow Democrat Jovanka Beckles in the November 6, 2018 general election, 53.6% to 46.4%; former President Barack Obama endorsed her in that general election. She was re-elected in 2020 with 84.7% against independent Sara Brink. After 2021 redistricting moved her seat to District 14, she was re-elected in 2022 with 88.4% against Republican Rich Kinney, and in 2024 with 68.5% against fellow Democrat Margot Smith. (Source: Ballotpedia, Buffy Wicks.)

Wicks has made housing policy her signature legislative focus. She chaired the Assembly Housing and Community Development Committee for two years before becoming Chair of the Assembly Appropriations Committee in the 2025 to 2026 session, and in December 2025 Speaker Robert Rivas appointed her to chair a newly created Select Committee on Housing Construction Innovation, tasked with exploring lower-cost, climate-smart home construction methods. (Source: official Assembly biography; official Assembly press release, wicks.asmdc.org/press-releases, December 4, 2025.)

voting_record_highlights: AB 2011 (2022), the Affordable Housing and High Road Jobs Act of 2022, creating a ministerial, streamlined approval pathway for affordable and mixed-income housing on commercial corridors: Wicks was the lead author. Signed by Gov. Gavin Newsom on September 28, 2022 as Chapter 647, Statutes of 2022. Wicks's office announced a first-in-nation outcomes review of the law's implementation in February 2026. (Source: leginfo.legislature.ca.gov bill text for AB 2011, 2021 to 2022; official Assembly press release, February 3, 2026.)

AB 2023 (2025 to 2026), Companion chatbots: children's safety, introduced by Wicks and Assemblymember Rebecca Bauer-Kahan as the Assembly companion to Sen. Steve Padilla's SB 1119 ("Adam's Law"): as of the version amended in the Senate on June 17, 2026, AB 2023 had not been chaptered; SB 1119, the parallel Senate vehicle establishing the nation's most comprehensive child-safety standards for AI companion chatbots, was signed by Gov. Newsom on September 10, 2026. (Source: leginfo.legislature.ca.gov bill text and status for AB 2023, 2025 to 2026; official Assembly press release, September 10, 2026.)

ACA 22 (2025 to 2026), adding Section 4.5 to Article XIII A of the California Constitution to require a two-thirds vote for citizen-initiated local special taxes and to bar new local ad valorem property taxes: Wicks was the sole named author. It passed the Assembly 68-2 and the Senate 35-1 on June 25, 2026, the legislative deadline day, as part of a negotiated deal in which the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association and California Business Roundtable withdrew a considerably harsher, retroactive competing initiative from the same ballot. It was filed with the Secretary of State the same day as Chapter 132, Statutes of 2026, placing the measure before voters as Proposition 43. Wicks has publicly stated she authored it only to remove the harsher initiative from the ballot and does not want it to become law: "I authored ACA 22 not because I wanted it to become law — but because it was the only path left to get the more dangerous initiative off the ballot before time ran out." Full detail on the measure itself, the withdrawn competing initiative, and campaign finance is covered in content/measures/ca-prop-43-2026.json and is not duplicated here. (Sources: leginfo.legislature.ca.gov bill text for ACA 22, 2025 to 2026; Ballotpedia, California Proposition 43, Two-Thirds Vote Requirement for Local Special Tax Initiatives and Property Tax Initiative Prohibition Amendment (2026).)
attendance: No individually published floor-attendance or voting-participation record for Assemblymember Wicks was found. The California State Assembly does not publish a per-member attendance scorecard; the only public records are bill-by-bill roll-call votes at leginfo.legislature.ca.gov, which is what the voting-record entries above are drawn from.
